reasoning:
Both outputs are strong, both commit to a point of view, and both independently land the same best insight (the defensible layer for a non-designer tool is judgment/sign-off, which Figma is structurally disinclined to build because saying 'is this safe to ship?' to a professional designer is an insult). A wins on two dimensions that the eval prompt explicitly asks for. First, separating what actually changed from what was merely announced: A knows the agent is in beta as of 20 May 2026, rolling out in waves, free now and metered by AI credits at general availability, and — critically — that Full seats on Professional/Organization/Enterprise get it in all design files while Dev and Collab seats get it only in draft files. I verified that seat gating almost verbatim against Figma's own launch blog, and the credit language verbatim ('During beta, the agent won't consume credits. AI credits will apply at general availability'). A builds its central argument on that gate ('Figma has shipped a capability the non-designer structurally cannot reach in a real file, and is about to meter it'), then correctly names it as revocable and sizes the window at 12-18 months. B never registers that the agent is in beta, wave-gated, seat-gated, or not yet metered, and so treats an announcement as a fully-available capability — for a document whose job is sizing a competitive threat to this exact segment, that is the most decision-relevant fact in the launch and it is missing. Second, strategic range: A works through roughly eight distinct lenses (launch mechanics, business model and why-now, threat reframing, winners/losers including non-obvious ones, first/second/third-order consequences, two bear cases, a paired historical analogy that points both ways, and scored plays). B is essentially one thesis (the missing constraint layer) developed rigorously, plus one good lateral move (the real attacker is prompt-to-app from below, not Figma) — deeper, but narrower.

On factual accuracy, which the caller flagged as decisive: I web-verified thirteen checkable claims in A and five in B. A's load-bearing claims all hold. Q1 FY2026 revenue of $333.4M, up 46% YoY, with net dollar retention at 139% described as the highest in over two years — confirmed exactly against Figma's SEC 8-K and earnings materials. A's inference that credits convert a seat business into seats-plus-usage is corroborated beyond what A claimed: the same earnings call attributes growth to 'early traction from AI credit monetization, which started on March 18th' and raised full-year guidance by $55M on AI monetization. A's bear case that metered credits are hostile to iteration is corroborated by real Figma forum complaints about Make burning credits on exactly the iterative fixing that constitutes the work. Figma Sites publishing requiring a Full seat — confirmed on Figma's pricing page. The 91% designer-sentiment stat is real (Figma's State of the Designer 2026, n=906), though it is precisely 91% of designers who increased AI usage rather than all surveyed; A slightly overstates the denominator but uses the stat only to discount it, explicitly flagging it as an incumbent self-report of its own users.

A does carry two real errors. Its claim that 'shared libraries live on Organization and Enterprise' is false — team-wide design libraries are available on Professional and above per Figma's pricing page. This weakens A's tier-differentiation mechanism in the 'why now' section, but it is a secondary argument, not the foundation of the recommendation. And 'Canva shipped AI 2.0 in March 2026' is off by a month — Canva AI 2.0 launched at Canva Create on 16 April 2026, though the proprietary Canva Design Model underneath it is real and A's substantive point (Canva, not Figma, is the compression threat from below) is sound; March is plausibly a conflation with Magic Layers' public beta. A also omits a fact that cuts against its own thesis: Figma now offers an $8/month Content seat giving non-designers access to the Sites CMS, which softens the 'structurally cannot reach it' framing.

B, by contrast, has no detected factual errors — but over a much smaller and less load-bearing set of claims. Figma Sites publishing live responsive sites with a CMS, Figma Make going prompt-to-interactive-web-app, and the agent generating real artboards from canvas are all confirmed. B's claim that 'independent testing reports it is strongest at flows built on a real, component-based design system' accurately represents its cited source, which does report the sweet spot as mobile flows on a component-based design system with everything outside that being where the agent struggles. Calling one personal blog 'independent testing' is slightly generous framing, but B honestly separates it from 'Figma's own positioning,' and B selectively omits that the same source found the agent's default output to be generic slop with inconsistent token binding — an omission that would actually have helped B's argument.

Source labeling: A is the better of the two here, and explicitly so. It closes with tiered corroboration guidance — treat launch mechanics and seat tiers as well-corroborated, revenue figures as single-source, the designer survey as an incumbent self-report — which is exactly the right hygiene, and conservative, since the revenue figures are in fact an SEC filing. B opens with an honest 'what I checked, and what I'm taking on faith' section and executes the single best epistemic move in either document: it verifies Figma Sites and Make, discovers this kills the argument it was about to make ('their output is a design file, ours is a live thing, we're safe. That's false'), and tells the reader not to make that argument in a strategy meeting.

Where B is genuinely better: it is more executable. Section 4's decomposition into Deriver / Composer / Ship-check with independent testability, the two-week throwaway derivation test against 30 real customer URLs graded blind, and kill criteria stated in advance 'so we can't rationalize later' are a sharper falsification plan than anything in A. B's stress test correctly identifies that derived constraints may not beat good defaults. If the question were 'what do we do Monday,' B answers it better. The prompt was 'riff on this with me,' which is the other question — and B explicitly declares it is not doing a riff and is running the heavy version instead, an honest override but an override nonetheless. A stays closer to the requested register while still resolving into a scored 90-day recommendation, names the tempting dud move ('building a better prompt-to-screen generator... name it dead in the room'), and closes with three data questions carrying explicit decision thresholds.

Both stress tests are honest. A's is the better-calibrated of the two: it names that its entire argument rests on a competitor pricing decision revocable in a single release note, and lets a hypothetical Canva strategist land the hardest blow on the document itself. Net: A on strategic range, on separating shipped from announced, and on a far larger verified factual base with explicit source tiering; B is the safer, more executable, error-free document that misses the launch mechanics that matter most to its own segment.
